analysis.one_liner: Lets workers form a union by signed cards instead of an election, with penalties for employers who interfere.
analysis.headline: 215 House members backed the bill, including 199 of the chamber's 202 Democrats, but it never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would change how workers form unions. If a majority of employees at a workplace signed cards saying they wanted a union, the National Labor Relations Board would certify the union directly instead of running a secret-ballot election. It would also push employers and new unions to reach a first contract, with a mediator and then binding arbitration if they stalled, and it would raise penalties for employers who fire or threaten workers during organizing drives.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to form unions gain the most. They would no longer have to win an election that employers can contest and delay for months, and workers fired or threatened for organizing would get triple back pay plus fines against the employer of up to $20,000 per violation.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers trying to organize a union

how_it_helps.text: If a majority of employees in a bargaining unit sign cards authorizing a union, the NLRB must certify that union without holding an election, eliminating the election campaign period in which most employer interference occurs.

After a union is certified, the parties must start bargaining within 10 days; if no agreement is reached after 90 days of bargaining and 30 days of mediation, the dispute goes to binding arbitration, whose award governs the first contract for two years. This prevents employers from simply refusing to agree to a first contract.

Employers who discriminate against employees during an organizing drive would owe back pay plus twice that amount in liquidated damages, and willful or repeated violators would face civil penalties of up to $20,000 per violation, where current law provides essentially no monetary penalty.

analysis.who_pays: Employers facing organizing campaigns bear the costs: they could no longer insist on an election they might delay or win, they would face binding arbitration over first contract terms they did not negotiate, and they would pay new fines and treble back pay for violations.

drawbacks.text: Majority sign-up would replace the secret-ballot election, so workers would publicly sign cards rather than vote privately; critics argue this exposes employees to pressure from union organizers and coworkers, and the bill itself requires the NLRB to establish procedures for verifying that signed cards are authentic.

Binding arbitration of first contracts means a government-appointed panel, not the employer or the union, would set wages and terms for the first two years of a new contract, which both sides in a negotiation could see as taking decisions out of their hands.

Employers would face substantially higher financial exposure during organizing drives, including treble back pay and fines up to $20,000 per violation, which businesses argued raises the stakes of any contested campaign.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits are large for workers who want a union: today, an employer can delay an election for months, campaign against the union, and unlawfully fire supporters while facing almost no penalty, and can then simply refuse to agree to a first contract. The bill targets all three of those steps. The main costs fall on employers, in the form of higher penalties and binding arbitration of first contract terms. The loss of the secret ballot is a genuine concern, though it applies only where a majority of workers have already signed public cards. On balance, the bill shifts power in union formation decisively from employers to workers.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and the Workforce Committee and then to a subcommittee, and it never received a markup or a floor vote before the 109th Congress ended.

narrative.text: George Miller introduced the Employee Free Choice Act in the House on April 19, 2005, and it was referred to the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
On May 9, 2005, the bill was referred to the Subcommittee on Employer-Employee Relations, and no further action was taken for the rest of the Congress.

The bill attracted 215 cosponsors: 199 of the House's 202 Democrats, 15 of 232 Republicans, and 1 Independent, meaning a numerical majority of the chamber supported it, yet it never reached the floor.
The Education and the Workforce Committee, controlled by the Republican majority, never reported the bill, and no version of the bill was voted on in either chamber during the 109th Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and the business groups that opposed union-friendly changes are better off, because a bill that would have raised organizing penalties and ended employer-controlled election timing died in committee without a vote. Workers who wanted an easier path to union formation gained nothing from this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers opposed to easier union formation

for.name: Rep. George Miller
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 19, 2005 with an initial slate of more than 100 original cosponsors and made introductory remarks on the House floor.

for.name: 199 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it support from nearly the entire House Democratic caucus plus 15 Republicans and 1 Independent.

for.name: Organized labor (AFL-CIO and affiliated unions)
for.what_they_did: Backed the Employee Free Choice Act as their top legislative priority and pushed for its passage.

against.name: Rep. John Boehner
against.role: Chair, House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled a markup or reported the bill out of committee, keeping it from the House floor for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Business groups led by the U.S. Chamber of Commerce
against.what_they_did: Campaigned against the bill, arguing that replacing elections with signed cards removes the secret ballot and that binding arbitration would let outsiders set contract terms.

against.name: 217 of 232 House Republicans
against.role: House Republicans who did not cosponsor
against.what_they_did: Declined to cosponsor the bill, leaving it without the Republican support needed to move it through a Republican-controlled committee.

sides.party_line_note: Support was almost entirely Democratic: 199 of the House's 202 Democrats signed on, versus 15 of 232 Republicans and 1 Independent, and no committee or floor vote ever tested the full chamber.

industries.note: The bill removes the election campaign employers can use to fight unions, imposes binding arbitration on first contracts, and adds fines up to $20,000 per violation plus triple back pay for retaliating against workers. These costs fall on businesses, while the protections run to workers exercising organizing rights.

Card-check certification and binding first-contract arbitration would make it much easier to organize new members and secure first contracts, and union membership gains historically translate into higher wages and benefits for the workers involved.
